paras: The White Hall sawmill whitecapping was the driving out of the Black workforce of the Davis and Hodges sawmill at White Hall, Poinsett County, Arkansas, by a band of white men on the morning of August 17, 1903. Eleven men described as prominent planters were arrested on federal charges, and in March 1904 a federal jury at Helena convicted three of them of conspiracy to intimidate Black workmen. The Cleveland Gazette called it the first such federal conviction in that section, and the defense appealed to the Supreme Court.
According to a Wynne dispatch to the Pine Bluff Daily Graphic, the Davis and Hodges mill was "operated exclusively by negro labor" in a community "thickly populated with negroes."

About 10 o'clock on the morning of August 17, eleven white men went to the mill in a body, unmasked, and ordered the Black workers out, "threatening them with violence if they did not leave at once." The Pine Bluff report named all eleven, among them three Parkers, two Staffords, S. W. McKinney and W. R. Clampit, most of them "well to do planters." The workers left at once, and the owners were forced to suspend business.

At the mill owner's instigation, Deputy United States Marshal U. G. Copeland took the eleven through Wynne to Helena on August 21. They were bound over to the federal grand jury under $1,000 bonds on a charge of conspiracy.

In October Judge Trieber told the grand jury at Helena that federal law forbade conspiring to keep any citizen from honest labor "on account of his being a negro." The grand jury indicted twenty-seven men: fifteen from Poinsett County in the sawmill case and twelve from Cross County, who were accused in a separate case of trying to drive Black people from that county.

In March 1904 the jury found three defendants guilty, recommending mercy, and discharged the other twelve. The three were Reuben Hodges, William Clampit and Wash McKinney. Judge Jacob Trieber sentenced them on March 19, and the defense appealed to the Supreme Court, claiming the statute enforcing the Fourteenth Amendment gave Black citizens a protection in federal courts not given to white men.

White papers carried the arrests mainly as a short wire item from Wynne, first printed as a Memphis Commercial Appeal special in the Birmingham Age-Herald on August 22. The same lines ran as far as Utah, Kansas and Vermont, calling the accused "prominent white planters," and one-line versions appeared in digests in Texas, Pennsylvania and Rhode Island. Only the Pine Bluff Daily Graphic printed a full account, including the owners' view that the attack came from "personal enemies, or grudge" against them.

The Vicksburg Herald, quoted in the Hattiesburg Daily Progress, welcomed the October indictments of the "night raiders" of Cross and Poinsett counties as a likely end to "the abominable business in Arkansas." The sentencing went out on the wire from Helena under headlines such as "Whitecaps Sentenced," with subheads that stressed the appeal as a test of the Fourteenth Amendment.

No Black-press report of the August incident was found; Black papers took up the case at the conviction. The Baltimore Afro-American and the Cleveland Gazette ran the sentencing in their news digests, the Afro-American describing the victims as "colored workmen." Under the heading "Convicted Ringleaders," the Cleveland Gazette also called the verdict a first for that section and gave the motive as "white men wanting their places." The Wichita Searchlight printed a later Helena dispatch, headed "Men Terrorized Negroes Are Sentenced in Arkansas," that named the mill and gave each man's sentence.

Counts differ: eleven in most August reports, twelve in the Topeka State Journal's wire copy, and fifteen Poinsett defendants at indictment and trial. Reuben Hodges is not in the August list of eleven, which has a "Rube Parker," and shares a surname with a mill owner; the coverage does not explain either point. Wire reports said all three men went to the penitentiary, but the later, itemized Wichita Searchlight dispatch gave Hodges and Clampit a year and a day in the Atlanta penitentiary and McKinney sixty days in the Lee County jail, each with a $100 fine.

reader.title: White Hall sawmill whitecapping
bases: A band of white planters drove the Black workforce from a sawmill under threat, and every report and the federal charge call it whitecapping (A5, A1, A17).
Two Wynne dispatches agree on the core event (A1, A5), and the federal indictment and conviction confirm it (A17, A25, A29).

accounts.gist: Black laborers at a Poinsett County sawmill were forced to leave under threats of violence by a band of white planters; eleven prominent planters were arrested at the mill owner's instigation.

accounts.label: Pine Bluff Daily Graphic correspondent
accounts.gist: Eleven named white men went to the Davis and Hodges mill unmasked about 10 a.m. on Aug. 17 and ordered the Black workers out under threat of violence; the mill shut down.

accounts.label: Mill owners' view
accounts.gist: Davis and Hodges believed the attack was the work of personal enemies or a grudge against them, since no other Black people in the area were bothered.

accounts.label: Federal charge
accounts.gist: The defendants conspired to intimidate Black workmen, threatening them with death if they did not leave the community.

accounts.label: Black correspondent
accounts.gist: Fifteen prominent Poinsett citizens had been indicted for making Black men quit work at a sawmill because white men wanted their places; three ringleaders were convicted.

accounts.label: Defense claim on appeal
accounts.gist: The federal statute gave Black citizens a protection in federal courts not given to white men, and so was challenged as unconstitutional.

framing.detail: Brief wire items headed 'Whitecappers Arrested' call the accused 'prominent white planters' and give no account from the workers.
The Pine Bluff Daily Graphic names the accused, calls the mill owners 'highly respected gentlemen' and reports their grudge theory.
The Vicksburg Herald, quoted in Hattiesburg, welcomes indictments of 'night raiders' and calls whitecapping an 'abominable business'.
Sentencing wire ('"Whitecappers" Sentenced', 'Whitecaps Sentenced') puts the Supreme Court test of the Fourteenth Amendment in its subhead.
The Cleveland Gazette heads its item 'Convicted Ringleaders', calls the verdict a first, and says white men wanted the Black workers' places.
The Wichita Searchlight runs the sentences under 'Men Terrorized Negroes Are Sentenced in Arkansas' and 'Whitecappers to Atlanta Pen'.
The Baltimore Afro-American and the Cleveland Gazette digest run one-sentence sentencing items.

A band of neighboring white planters, not the workers' employers; the mill owners pressed the prosecution
ordered_out, driven_out and threat (of violence; of death per the federal charge) are supported; no weapons are mentioned, and the men came unmasked in daylight
